title_en: Burundi Calls for Stronger International Action Over Continued Violence in Eastern DRC
excerpt_en: Bujumbura, June 4, 2026 - Burundi has urged the international community to increase its engagement in addressing the ongoing insecurity in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, citing continued fighting and what it describes as non-compliance with the Washington Peace Agreement.
body_en:
Bujumbura, June 4, 2026 - Burundi has urged the international community to increase its engagement in addressing the ongoing insecurity in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, citing continued fighting and what it describes as non-compliance with the Washington Peace Agreement.

The appeal was made by Burundi’s Minister of Foreign Affairs, Regional Integration and Development Cooperation, Édouard Bizimana, during talks held on June 1 with his Congolese counterpart, Floribert Anzuluni, in Bujumbura.

Bizimana expressed concern that despite diplomatic efforts linked to the Washington process-facilitated by international partners including the United States-violence involving the Congolese army and the AFC/M23 rebellion continues in parts of eastern DRC. He said the persistence of hostilities has led to renewed displacement and insecurity in several areas.

He also noted that while some progress has been made, including the return of displaced populations in certain regions, other zones remain unstable, calling for stronger international coordination to support regional peace initiatives.

During the same meeting, both ministers reaffirmed the importance of strengthening bilateral relations between Burundi and the Democratic Republic of the Congo and discussed broader cooperation issues, including diplomatic infrastructure, regional integration mechanisms, and preparations for upcoming regional summits within the International Conference on the Great Lakes Region (ICGLR).

Congolese Minister Floribert Anzuluni welcomed Burundi’s continued diplomatic and humanitarian support, particularly its assistance to Congolese refugees hosted in Burundi.

Burundi reiterated its commitment to regional peace efforts and its role within African Union frameworks aimed at stabilizing conflict-affected areas.

The statement comes amid ongoing tensions in eastern DRC, where multiple armed actors remain active despite repeated ceasefire agreements and international mediation efforts. Both Kinshasa and regional partners continue to accuse various parties of violating peace commitments, further complicating implementation of the Washington agreement.

body_en:
Rwanda, June 4, 2026 - U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio has stated that recent sanctions are beginning to influence Rwanda’s compliance with the Washington Agreement aimed at resolving the conflict in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo.

Speaking before the House Foreign Affairs Committee, Rubio said that while the peace agreement between Rwanda and the Democratic Republic of the Congo remains in place, its implementation has faced serious challenges, prompting Washington to impose targeted sanctions.

He noted that early signs suggest Rwanda has begun adjusting its position in response to these measures, although he acknowledged that progress remains slow and incomplete.

Rubio also emphasized that the situation in eastern Congo is not limited to state-to-state tensions, pointing to the continued activity of the AFC/M23 rebellion as a key unresolved issue within the broader peace framework.

He added that the United States expects the withdrawal of Rwandan forces from eastern DRC to take place within a set timeline, while warning that full stabilization will also depend on addressing the role of armed groups operating in the region.

The remarks come amid ongoing diplomatic tensions surrounding the implementation of the Washington Agreement, which was intended to reduce hostilities in the Great Lakes region but has instead been marked by mutual accusations of non-compliance.

In recent months, Washington has imposed a series of sanctions targeting individuals and military-linked actors connected to the conflict, as part of broader efforts to pressure parties toward adherence to the peace process.

body_en:
Kinshasa, June 3, 2026 - Economic and social activity slowed significantly across several parts of Kinshasa on Wednesday morning following the opposition’s call for a “ghost town” day aimed at protesting proposed constitutional amendments and alleged plans to extend President Félix Tshisekedi’s time in office.

The usually bustling capital awoke to unusually quiet streets, reduced public transport, shuttered businesses, and a visible security deployment in several communes. Major roads that are typically congested during morning rush hours saw lighter traffic, while schools, markets, and commercial centers operated at minimal capacity.

In the Mont-Amba district, roads leading to the University of Kinshasa remained unusually empty, with few students visible and public transport stops largely deserted. Security forces, including police officers and military vehicles, were deployed along major roads and near strategic locations.

In Limete, known for chronic traffic congestion, movement was noticeably reduced. Few vehicles circulated along Lumumba Boulevard and surrounding roads, while several residents reportedly kept their vehicles parked amid fears of unrest. Security patrols intensified in key areas, including First Street and major intersections.

The Tshangu district, one of Kinshasa’s most densely populated areas, also experienced significantly reduced activity. Commercial centers remained largely closed, public transportation was limited, and roads that are typically crowded saw lighter movement. Security forces, including police and members of the Republican Guard, maintained a heavy presence around administrative buildings and major access routes.

Small groups of political activists from both opposition and ruling party circles were observed in some neighborhoods, though no major mobilization was immediately visible. Some opposition supporters attempted symbolic demonstrations, while youth affiliated with the ruling party publicly encouraged residents to continue daily activities.

Across major arteries including Lumumba Boulevard, Victoire Roundabout, and parts of Kalamu, authorities deployed police and military personnel to monitor the situation and deter unrest. Despite the heightened security environment, movement remained generally calm throughout the morning.

The opposition had called for the stay-at-home protest to reject proposed constitutional reforms, which critics claim could pave the way for an extension of presidential rule. Authorities, however, maintained that Wednesday remained a normal working day, encouraging citizens to go about their activities.

body_en:
Butembo, June 9, 2026 - The Bishop of the Butembo-Beni Diocese, Paluku Sikuli, has voiced deep concern over worsening insecurity in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, condemning recurring massacres attributed to the Allied Democratic Forces (ADF) and criticizing what he described as political indifference to the suffering of civilians.

In a pastoral message issued from Butembo, the Catholic Church painted a grim picture of insecurity in the Beni, Lubero, and surrounding areas, where recent violence has reportedly claimed the lives of nearly 40 civilians and three police officers. The bishop warned that communities in the region are increasingly trapped between armed violence and growing instability.

According to Bishop Sikuli, the southern pastoral zone remains under the control of the M23 rebellion, while northern areas continue to suffer deadly attacks by ADF fighters. He said the persistent insecurity is not only costing lives but also crippling essential services and disrupting daily life for affected communities.

The bishop also criticized national political leaders, expressing concern that political priorities appear disconnected from the realities facing populations affected by violence. He urged authorities to focus on restoring peace and addressing urgent humanitarian and security needs rather than engaging in divisive political debates.

Bishop Sikuli called on President Félix Tshisekedi to prioritize peace and security across the country, stressing that governance should serve the protection and well-being of citizens. He also appealed to lawmakers to avoid political actions that ignore the hardships endured by civilians in conflict zones.

At the same time, he encouraged citizens to remain vigilant against political manipulation and urged security forces to reassess their operational approaches to better protect civilians and safeguard territorial integrity.

The bishop’s remarks follow a series of deadly attacks blamed on ADF rebels, including violence that killed 21 civilians in and around Beni, followed by another attack days later in Mbau that left at least 16 more civilians dead after earlier assaults in villages in Mambasa territory.

body_en:
Kinshasa, June 14, 2026 - President Félix Tshisekedi has instructed the Ministry of Defense and the Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC) to develop a detailed implementation plan for the training of Congolese soldiers in Egypt, following his official visit to Cairo earlier this week.

The directive was issued after Tshisekedi briefed the Council of Ministers on the outcomes of his June 10-11 visit to Egypt, held at the invitation of Egyptian President Abdel Fattah El-Sisi. The visit focused on strengthening bilateral cooperation between the two countries across several strategic sectors.

According to discussions presented during the Council of Ministers meeting, the two leaders agreed to deepen cooperation in areas including investment, diplomacy, urban development, health, and defense, with an emphasis on achieving practical results for both nations.

Military cooperation emerged as a key component of the agreements, with both countries committing to expand defense ties through a training program for Congolese military personnel in Egypt. President Tshisekedi subsequently tasked the Deputy Prime Minister in charge of Defense, in coordination with FARDC leadership, with preparing the necessary measures and submitting a detailed roadmap for implementation.

The initiative marks a new phase in military cooperation between Kinshasa and Cairo as the Democratic Republic of Congo continues efforts to modernize its armed forces and strengthen operational capacity amid persistent insecurity in the eastern part of the country.

The move comes as Congolese authorities continue to confront ongoing armed violence, including clashes involving the AFC/M23 rebellion in parts of North and South Kivu, while seeking broader regional partnerships to reinforce national defense capabilities.

title_en: AFC/M23 Condemns Tshisekedi's Houston Remarks as Threat to Peace Efforts
excerpt_en: Goma, June 18, 2026 - The AFC/M23 has strongly criticized President Félix Tshisekedi over remarks he made in Houston, United States, accusing him of undermining ongoing peace efforts and signaling a preference for a military solution to the conflict in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo.
body_en:
Goma, June 18, 2026 - The AFC/M23 has strongly criticized President Félix Tshisekedi over remarks he made in Houston, United States, accusing him of undermining ongoing peace efforts and signaling a preference for a military solution to the conflict in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo.

In a statement issued in Goma, AFC/M23 political coordinator Corneille Nangaa described the president's comments as an "irresponsible" and "warmongering" declaration made despite ongoing negotiations and an agreed ceasefire protocol.

According to Nangaa, Tshisekedi's assertion that government forces were making progress against their opponents and would soon retake Goma and Bukavu demonstrated a commitment to military action rather than dialogue.

He argued that such statements threaten diplomatic initiatives aimed at resolving the conflict and undermine mediation efforts.

Nangaa also warned that AFC/M23 would defend itself against any military action launched by government forces, saying the movement would respond to what it considers threats from Kinshasa.

The exchange comes as peace initiatives continue to seek a lasting ceasefire and renewed dialogue between the Congolese government and AFC/M23. However, fighting and tensions have persisted on the ground, with both sides maintaining differing interpretations of the commitments made under the peace process.

excerpt: Kinshasa, June 21, 2026 - The Democratic Republic of the Congo says recent reports on the security situation and mineral exploitation in eastern DRC have reinforced its legal and economic efforts against Rwanda and the AFC/M23.
title_en: DRC Says Rights Reports Strengthen Legal and Economic Case Against Rwanda and AFC/M23
excerpt_en: Kinshasa, June 21, 2026 - The Democratic Republic of the Congo says recent reports on the security situation and mineral exploitation in eastern DRC have reinforced its legal and economic efforts against Rwanda and the AFC/M23.
body_en:
Kinshasa, June 21, 2026 - The Democratic Republic of the Congo says recent reports on the security situation and mineral exploitation in eastern DRC have reinforced its legal and economic efforts against Rwanda and the AFC/M23.

Government spokesperson Patrick Muyaya said the findings support information already gathered by Congolese authorities and will strengthen ongoing legal actions. He announced that the Ministry of Justice is preparing additional judicial measures in the coming days.

Muyaya said the government's strategy targets both legal accountability and the economic networks linked to the exploitation and trade of minerals from conflict-affected areas. He stressed that investigations should examine the entire mineral supply chain rather than focusing only on those extracting the resources.

He also said the reports could provide additional evidence for existing legal proceedings concerning alleged war crimes and other violations committed in eastern DRC.

Addressing allegations of child recruitment, Muyaya stated that authorities had received repeated reports from families claiming children were being forcibly recruited in areas under AFC/M23 control. He argued that coercive recruitment reflects the group's difficulty in gaining public support in territories it controls.

The government reaffirmed its intention to continue pursuing legal, diplomatic, and economic measures aimed at protecting the country's interests and combating what it describes as an economy driven by conflict in eastern DRC.

Kinshasa maintains that the prolonged instability in the region is fueled by the illegal exploitation of mineral resources. Rwanda has consistently denied allegations that it is involved in exploiting Congolese minerals or supporting instability in eastern DRC.

Speaking during a live discussion, Nshole rejected accusations that the Catholic Church supports armed groups, insisting that the Church has consistently condemned rebellion and repeatedly urged the government to invest in building a strong national army.

title: DRC and Rwanda Reaffirm Commitment to Peace Agreement and De-escalation in Minembwe
excerpt: London, June 25, 2026 - The Democratic Republic of the Congo and Rwanda have reaffirmed their commitment to fully implementing the June 27, 2025 peace agreement and to taking immediate steps to reduce tensions in the Minembwe area.
title_en: DRC and Rwanda Reaffirm Commitment to Peace Agreement and De-escalation in Minembwe
excerpt_en: London, June 25, 2026 - The Democratic Republic of the Congo and Rwanda have reaffirmed their commitment to fully implementing the June 27, 2025 peace agreement and to taking immediate steps to reduce tensions in the Minembwe area.
body_en:
London, June 25, 2026 - The Democratic Republic of the Congo and Rwanda have reaffirmed their commitment to fully implementing the June 27, 2025 peace agreement and to taking immediate steps to reduce tensions in the Minembwe area.

The commitments were announced following the sixth meeting of the Joint Oversight Committee, which brought together representatives from the DRC, Rwanda, the United States, Qatar, Togo, acting as the African Union mediator, and the African Union Commission.

Participants expressed concern over the escalation of fighting in eastern DRC, the impact of drone strikes on civilians, and the worsening humanitarian situation, including the ongoing Ebola outbreak. They stressed the need to ensure that the ceasefire is fully respected.

excerpt_en: Kinshasa, June 27, 2026 - One year after the signing of the Washington Peace Agreement between the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Rwanda, implementation has remained limited, with the two countries completing less than one-third of their respective commitments, according to an independent asse
body_en:
Kinshasa, June 27, 2026 - One year after the signing of the Washington Peace Agreement between the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Rwanda, implementation has remained limited, with the two countries completing less than one-third of their respective commitments, according to an independent assessment.

The agreement, signed on June 27, 2025, was designed to promote peace and stability in the Great Lakes region through the neutralization of armed groups, the withdrawal of foreign forces, enhanced security cooperation, and regional economic integration.

An annual evaluation found that only 35% of the agreement's overall commitments had been implemented during its first year. Of the 30 identified tasks, 22 showed some level of progress, ranging from initial implementation to full completion.

The Democratic Republic of the Congo completed 31.7% of the commitments assigned to it, while Rwanda reached 30.6%. The international partners involved in supporting the agreement-including the United States, Qatar, the African Union, and other stakeholders-recorded the highest implementation rate at 53.5%.

The assessment noted that implementation progressed rapidly during the first two months after the agreement was signed before slowing considerably toward the end of 2025. Progress remained largely stagnant between December 2025 and February 2026 before modest improvements resumed in the following months.

Several factors were cited for the limited progress, including an imbalance in implementation priorities, with greater attention given to institutional and economic measures than key security commitments. Persistent mistrust between the parties also slowed the fulfillment of interdependent obligations.

Operations aimed at neutralizing the FDLR began only in late March 2026, while continued clashes between the Congolese army and the AFC/M23, along with delays in deploying the Expanded Joint Verification Mechanism Plus (EJVM+), further hindered implementation.

The report also highlighted that the worsening humanitarian and security situation in eastern DRC continues to undermine efforts to implement the agreement, despite repeated diplomatic initiatives.

Bamako, June 1, 2026 - Mali and the West African Economic and Monetary Union (UEMOA) have reinforced agricultural cooperation following high-level talks focused on the launch of a strategic white paper targeting key agricultural sectors across the region.

Mali’s Minister of Agriculture, Dr Ibrahima Samake, accompanied by senior officials from his ministry, received a delegation from the UEMOA Commission led by Commissioner Paul Koffi Koffi, responsible for the Department of Business Development, Mines, Energy, and the Digital Economy.

The mission aimed to present and officially launch UEMOA’s white paper dedicated to three priority sectors considered critical to regional agricultural transformation: phosphate and fertilizers, rice production, and textile cotton.

The initiative is designed to enhance agricultural production and productivity across UEMOA member states through an investment portfolio estimated at 6,000 billion CFA francs over a 15-year period from 2026 to 2040.

During the meeting, Minister Samake highlighted the strategic importance Mali places on the initiative, emphasizing its alignment with broader regional ambitions to position agriculture as a key driver of economic growth and sustainable development within UEMOA member countries.

body_en:
Djibouti, June 10, 2026 - Under the chairmanship of President Ismaïl Omar Guelleh, Head of Government, the 6th session of the Council of Ministers was held on June 9, 2026, focusing on a wide range of legislative, economic, institutional, and social reforms across key sectors of national development.

At the opening of the session, the Head of State expressed gratitude to the Djiboutian population, government members, and international partners for their support following the death of Madame Nazli Abdallah Mohamed Kamil, offering prayers for the deceased.

The Council reviewed and approved several draft laws and decrees presented by various ministries, covering public enterprises, social protection systems, justice reforms, education policy, and public land allocation.

From the Ministry of Energy and Natural Resources, the Council approved the financial statements of Electricité de Djibouti (EDD) for the 2024 fiscal year. The utility reported revenues of over 41.9 billion FDJ and expenses of approximately 40.5 billion FDJ, resulting in a surplus of 1.46 billion FDJ. Officials noted increased electricity demand in Djibouti City, alongside rising operating costs and continued investment in energy production, including interconnection, diesel, and wind power.

The Ministry of Labor and Social Protection presented the 2023 financial accounts of the National Social Security Fund (CNSS), which recorded a surplus of 3.58 billion FDJ. While slightly lower than the previous year, the institution maintained stable revenues supported by contributions and financial income, alongside ongoing investments in infrastructure projects, including preparations related to a new hospital.

In the justice sector, the Council examined a decree acknowledging the resignation of magistrate Issam Kalid Abdallah and a separate decree authorizing him to practice law, in accordance with national legal provisions.

The Ministry of Higher Education and Research announced the appointment of Dr. Madina Daher Okiye as President of the University of Djibouti, replacing Dr. Djama Mohamed Hassan, marking a leadership transition within the country’s principal academic institution.

The Ministry of National Education extended for five years the legal framework governing the “High School Graduation Certificate,” a qualification designed for international and specialized education institutions. The measure aims to maintain continuity for programs such as those at the Horn of Africa School while supporting inclusive education policies, including for refugee students.

excerpt: Djibouti City, June 18, 2026 - Djibouti's President Ismaïl Omar Guelleh joined a high-level virtual meeting of African heads of state and government to coordinate the regional response to the Ebola outbreak affecting the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) and Uganda.
title_en: African Leaders Coordinate Ebola Response as President Guelleh Joins High-Level Virtual Summit
excerpt_en: Djibouti City, June 18, 2026 - Djibouti's President Ismaïl Omar Guelleh joined a high-level virtual meeting of African heads of state and government to coordinate the regional response to the Ebola outbreak affecting the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) and Uganda.
body_en:
Djibouti City, June 18, 2026 - Djibouti's President Ismaïl Omar Guelleh joined a high-level virtual meeting of African heads of state and government to coordinate the regional response to the Ebola outbreak affecting the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) and Uganda.

The meeting focused on the evolving epidemiological situation following the declaration of the outbreak in the DRC one month earlier, as leaders expressed concern over the pace of transmission and the challenges facing response efforts in affected areas.

Participants reviewed the latest figures from the two affected countries, with the Democratic Republic of the Congo reporting 695 confirmed Ebola cases, including 138 deaths, while Uganda had recorded 19 confirmed cases and two fatalities.

Discussions centered on strengthening disease control measures, particularly in eastern DRC, including the provinces of Ituri, North Kivu, and South Kivu. Leaders emphasized the importance of expanding testing, improving contact tracing, reinforcing epidemiological surveillance, and enhancing regional cooperation to contain the outbreak, especially in conflict-affected areas where access for health workers remains difficult.

The virtual summit brought together several African leaders, including Évariste Ndayishimiye, Chairperson of the African Union; Cyril Ramaphosa; Duma Boko; Azali Assoumani; Teodoro Obiang Nguema Mbasogo; Emmerson Mnangagwa; and Mahamoud Ali Youssouf.

Also participating was António Guterres, reflecting the international significance of the outbreak and the need for coordinated global support.

President Guelleh, who currently chairs the Intergovernmental Authority on Development (IGAD), was accompanied during the meeting by Foreign Affairs Minister Aboulkader Houssein Omar, Health Minister Mouna Osman Aden, and Presidential Diplomatic Adviser Fathia Djama Oudine.

The discussions underscored the importance of regional solidarity and coordinated action to strengthen surveillance, improve outbreak response, and prevent further cross-border transmission of Ebola in East and Central Africa.

title_en: Ethiopia-Djibouti Partnership Strengthens Regional Integration in the Horn of Africa
excerpt_en: Djibouti City, June 23, 2026 - Ethiopia and Djibouti continue to deepen a strategic partnership that has evolved into one of the Horn of Africa's strongest examples of regional integration, driven by growing economic interdependence, infrastructure development, and cooperation on security and trade.
body_en:
Djibouti City, June 23, 2026 - Ethiopia and Djibouti continue to deepen a strategic partnership that has evolved into one of the Horn of Africa's strongest examples of regional integration, driven by growing economic interdependence, infrastructure development, and cooperation on security and trade.

The relationship, built on longstanding historical, cultural, and economic ties, has expanded significantly over the past decades from a focus on maritime access to a broad partnership encompassing transport, energy, telecommunications, water resources, and regional security.

Djibouti remains Ethiopia's principal maritime gateway, handling the vast majority of the country's international trade. The partnership has been reinforced through major infrastructure investments, including the Addis Ababa-Djibouti standard-gauge railway, expanded road corridors, modernized dry ports, and improved customs systems that have enhanced cross-border trade and logistics.

Cooperation has also grown in other strategic sectors. Ethiopia supplies electricity to Djibouti through cross-border power interconnections, while joint water infrastructure projects have strengthened regional cooperation in public services. These initiatives have contributed to increasing economic interdependence between the two neighboring countries.

As Ethiopia's economy and population continue to expand, both countries are working to improve regional transport networks and diversify trade corridors to support long-term economic growth and resilience. These efforts align with broader regional integration objectives promoted by the African Union and the Intergovernmental Authority on Development (IGAD).

The partnership has taken on added significance amid evolving geopolitical dynamics in the Red Sea and the Horn of Africa. Rising regional tensions and disruptions to international shipping have highlighted the strategic importance of the Ethiopia-Djibouti transport corridor as a key route connecting the region to global markets.

Beyond economic cooperation, Djibouti and Ethiopia have strengthened collaboration on security through joint mechanisms addressing border management, intelligence sharing, and efforts to combat piracy, illicit trafficking, organized crime, and other transnational threats affecting the region.

The two countries increasingly view infrastructure development, coordinated economic policies, and institutional cooperation as essential tools for promoting regional stability and sustainable development. Their collaboration reflects a broader shift in the Horn of Africa toward greater economic integration and cross-border connectivity.

title: National Assembly Advances Ratification of African Development Bank Loan Agreement
excerpt: Djibouti City, June 25, 2026 - Djibouti's National Assembly has advanced the parliamentary process for ratifying a loan agreement with the African Development Bank (AfDB), moving the financing package one step closer to final approval.
title_en: National Assembly Advances Ratification of African Development Bank Loan Agreement
excerpt_en: Djibouti City, June 25, 2026 - Djibouti's National Assembly has advanced the parliamentary process for ratifying a loan agreement with the African Development Bank (AfDB), moving the financing package one step closer to final approval.
body_en:
Djibouti City, June 25, 2026 - Djibouti's National Assembly has advanced the parliamentary process for ratifying a loan agreement with the African Development Bank (AfDB), moving the financing package one step closer to final approval.

Meeting under the chairmanship of National Assembly Speaker Dileita Mohamed Dileita, the Conference of Presidents examined the draft ratification law under an emergency procedure in accordance with the Assembly's rules of procedure.

The session was attended by Acting Prime Minister and Minister of Justice, Penitentiary Affairs and Relations with Parliament, Ali Hassan Bahdon, representing the government. Also present were the First and Second Vice-Presidents of the National Assembly, chairpersons of the standing committees, and the General Rapporteur for the Budget.

Following its deliberations, the Conference of Presidents approved the referral of the draft law to the Foreign Affairs Committee for detailed examination and scheduled a plenary session for June 29, 2026, during which lawmakers will debate and vote on the agreement.

The Foreign Affairs Committee, chaired by Abdourahman Awaleh Yacin, immediately convened to review the proposed legislation under the expedited procedure.

The committee's deliberations were attended by Minister of Agriculture, Water, Fisheries, Livestock and Marine Resources Radwan Abdillahi Bahdon, accompanied by senior ministry officials, who briefed lawmakers on the objectives and significance of the financing agreement.

After reviewing the proposal, the committee issued a favorable opinion, endorsing the ratification of the loan agreement and recommending that it proceed to the plenary session for final consideration.

The latest parliamentary action brings Djibouti closer to completing the ratification process for the African Development Bank financing agreement, which is expected to support the country's development priorities through additional external funding.

title_en: Kuwait Restricts Worker Recruitment From Rwanda, Uganda and Kenya
excerpt_en: Kuwait City, June 10, 2026 - Kuwaiti authorities have published a revised list of countries from which companies are permitted to recruit foreign workers, placing Rwanda, Uganda, and Kenya among nations facing recruitment restrictions.
body_en:
Kuwait City, June 10, 2026 - Kuwaiti authorities have published a revised list of countries from which companies are permitted to recruit foreign workers, placing Rwanda, Uganda, and Kenya among nations facing recruitment restrictions.

The decision, announced by Kuwait’s Ministry of Interior, outlines countries approved for labor recruitment as part of efforts to regulate foreign employment and improve labor management systems in the Gulf nation.

Countries approved for worker recruitment include South Africa, Benin, Eritrea, Ethiopia, the Philippines, Sri Lanka, India, Vietnam, Nepal, and Senegal.

At the same time, Kuwait identified 27 countries from which recruitment by local companies is restricted. The list includes Rwanda, Uganda, Kenya, Burundi, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Angola, Madagascar, Liberia, Mali, Burkina Faso, Gambia, and Cameroon, among others.

Kuwaiti authorities said the decision was made following consultations involving the ministries responsible for foreign affairs and health, as well as the country’s labor regulatory agency.

Officials indicated that in some cases the restrictions apply specifically to female workers, while male workers from affected countries may continue to be eligible for employment opportunities.

The revised recruitment framework forms part of Kuwait’s broader efforts to address long-standing concerns surrounding the recruitment and management of foreign labor, a sector that has frequently faced criticism over inefficiencies and employment-related challenges.

Kuwait remains one of the major destinations in the Middle East for African migrant workers, many of whom are employed in domestic services, hospitality, industry, and restaurant sectors.

body_en:
Kigali, June 11, 2026 - Former Minister of Trade and Industry, Prudence Sebahizi, and former State Minister in the Ministry of Infrastructure, Jean de Dieu Uwihanganye, have expressed gratitude to President Paul Kagame following their replacement in the latest government reshuffle.

The changes, announced on the night of June 10, saw Sebahizi replaced at the Ministry of Trade and Industry by former Permanent Secretary at the ministry, Antoine Marie Kajangwe. Uwihanganye also left his position as State Minister in the Ministry of Infrastructure as part of the cabinet adjustments.

In a message shared after the announcement, Sebahizi thanked President Kagame for entrusting him with the role of Minister of Trade and Industry, a position he had held for two years. He highlighted achievements made alongside fellow ministers and ministry staff, particularly in advancing industrial development, private sector growth, trade integration, and regional cooperation.

Sebahizi described the progress achieved during his tenure as an important contribution to Rwanda’s economic development and extended congratulations to his successor, Kajangwe, expressing confidence in his ability to build on existing achievements.

Sebahizi had been appointed Minister of Trade and Industry on August 16, 2024, replacing Jean Chrysostome Ngabitsinze following cabinet appointments made by President Kagame.

Uwihanganye also issued a message of appreciation, thanking the president for the opportunity to serve, as well as for guidance and support received during his time in office. He praised the dedication and cooperation of staff at the Ministry of Infrastructure and affirmed his willingness to continue contributing to national development.

Uwihanganye joined the government in July 2025 after previously serving as Rwanda’s ambassador to Singapore.

Kigali, Rwanda, June 22, 2026 - Democratic Ideal Party (PDI) President Sheikh Musa Fazil Harerimana has questioned the Democratic Republic of the Congo's commitment to implementing its peace agreement with Rwanda, arguing that lasting cooperation will remain difficult unless armed groups operating in eastern DRC are dismantled.

Harerimana made the remarks on June 21 while addressing members during the party's annual General Assembly.

Speaking to journalists after the meeting, he said security challenges in the Great Lakes region continue to be driven by the presence of the Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Rwanda (FDLR), an armed group founded by individuals linked to the 1994 Genocide against the Tutsi.

He argued that some actors in the region have continued to support the group, undermining efforts to restore lasting peace and security.

Referring to the peace agreement signed between Rwanda and the Democratic Republic of the Congo in December 2025, Harerimana questioned whether the Congolese government had the political will to fully implement its commitments.

He said the agreement's success depends on fulfilling all of its provisions, including measures aimed at dismantling the FDLR and addressing the security concerns of both countries.

Harerimana also called on PDI members to understand the historical roots of the regional conflict and to counter misinformation through factual information and civic engagement.

During the meeting, Senator Hadidja Murangwa Ndangiza, chairperson of the Senate Committee on Foreign Affairs, National Unity and Security and a member of the PDI, described the agreement as an important opportunity to address the underlying causes of insecurity in the region.

Kinshasa, DRC, June 23, 2026 - The meeting between Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) President Félix Tshisekedi and Burundian President Évariste Ndayishimiye has drawn attention from regional observers, with some analysts linking the visit to the ongoing security situation in eastern DRC.

President Ndayishimiye began a two-day visit to Kinshasa on June 22, where he held talks with President Tshisekedi on bilateral relations and regional security, particularly the conflict in eastern DRC.

The visit comes as Burundian troops continue to operate in eastern DRC under a bilateral military cooperation agreement with Kinshasa, alongside Congolese forces in operations against armed groups.

Political analyst Tite Gatabazi said the timing of the visit coincides with intensified fighting in South Kivu, particularly around the Minembwe area, where clashes have recently escalated.

According to Gatabazi, the meeting was likely influenced by recent military developments on the ground. He argued that the two leaders share common security objectives in eastern DRC and suggested that the visit was intended to assess the situation following ongoing military operations.

Gatabazi further claimed that Congolese and Burundian forces had sought to secure control of Minembwe before the DRC's Independence Day on June 30, but that the objective had not been achieved. He also alleged that the recent fighting resulted in significant losses for both armies.

The governments of the DRC and Burundi have not publicly commented on these specific claims.

The Burundian military has maintained a presence in eastern DRC since 2022 under agreements with the Congolese government to conduct joint operations against armed groups operating in the region.

Dr. Nsengiyumva delivered the remarks via video conference during the opening of the Lesotho National Leadership Forum on June 22, where he was invited to discuss Rwanda's governance and development journey.

He thanked Lesotho for strengthening cooperation between the two countries and providing a platform for exchanging experiences on leadership and national development.

Reflecting on Rwanda's post-genocide recovery, the Prime Minister said the country chose to focus on building its future despite the widespread destruction of institutions, the economy and social fabric following the 1994 Genocide against the Tutsi.

He said one of Rwanda's most important lessons was the need to establish a clear long-term national vision, citing the implementation of Vision 2020 and the ongoing Vision 2050 strategy as frameworks that have guided development and improved living standards.

According to Dr. Nsengiyumva, long-term planning has enabled government institutions to work toward common national goals while maintaining policy consistency across sectors.

He also emphasized the importance of building on Rwanda's comparative strengths, including investment in tourism, sports, services and effective public administration, while maintaining strong economic management and a firm stance against corruption.

The Prime Minister stressed that citizen participation has been central to Rwanda's development model, saying sustainable progress can only be achieved when citizens actively contribute to national decision-making and implementation of government programs.

Officials warned that continued escalation risks deepening an already severe humanitarian crisis in the region, where access to food, shelter, and basic services remains critically limited.

body_en:
Geneva, June 15, 2026 - Sudan's Attorney General, Intisar Ahmed Abdel Aal, has called for greater international support to end the country's ongoing conflict, urging the United Nations Human Rights Council to back the government's efforts to restore peace and strengthen national accountability mechanisms.

Addressing the 62nd session of the UN Human Rights Council, Abdel Aal said Sudan had registered 149,860 legal cases related to crimes committed since the outbreak of the war, including 385 cases involving members of the regular armed forces whose legal immunity had been lifted.

She argued that Sudan's judicial institutions are capable of investigating and prosecuting violations and called for support for the National Committee for the Investigation of Crimes and Violations of National and International Humanitarian Law under the principle of complementarity. She also urged the Human Rights Council to end the mandate of the international Fact-Finding Mission, accusing it of politicizing its work.

The Attorney General further called for an immediate halt to external support for the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), alleging that foreign actors continue to provide assistance to the paramilitary group. She also appealed to states to prevent the recruitment, financing, and transfer of mercenaries into Sudan.

Abdel Aal accused the RSF of committing widespread violations against civilians, public infrastructure, and state institutions, including alleged war crimes, crimes against humanity, genocide, and serious breaches of national and international humanitarian law.

She said documented violations in Darfur and parts of Kordofan included killings, forced displacement, sexual violence, looting, abductions, and arbitrary detention in facilities allegedly operated by the RSF, including in El Fasher and Nyala.

According to figures presented during the session, investigators have documented 2,200 rape cases and 1,499 cases of detention and enforced disappearance since the conflict began.

The committee also reported that 30,071 people have been killed and 44,061 injured in documented violations. Of the nearly 150,000 legal cases registered, 6,158 were dismissed during investigations, while 21,787 cases were referred for trial and judicial rulings had been issued in 10,417 cases.

body_en:
El Obeid, June 22, 2026 - International organizations have warned that Sudan's North Kordofan capital, El Obeid, faces a growing risk of mass atrocities as the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) continue to build up forces around the city, raising fears of a large-scale ground assault.

The United Nations Security Council expressed deep concern over reports of the military buildup and called on the RSF to halt its offensive against the city. Council members also voiced alarm over the escalating violence across Sudan and warned that intensified fighting in the Kordofan region could further worsen an already severe humanitarian crisis.

The Council urged all parties to cease hostilities immediately, protect civilians, comply with international humanitarian law, and uphold commitments made under the Jeddah Declaration. It also called for investigations into alleged violations committed during the conflict and stressed the need for accountability.

The Security Council expressed concern over the increasing use of drones in the conflict, including reported RSF drone strikes targeting El Obeid, and urged all parties to facilitate safe humanitarian access and allow civilians to leave conflict zones without obstruction.

It also called on foreign governments to refrain from actions that could fuel the conflict and reaffirmed its support for Sudan's sovereignty, territorial integrity, and unity while rejecting the establishment of parallel governing authorities.

The European Union issued a separate warning, urging that El Obeid must not be allowed to suffer the same fate as El Fasher, where a major RSF offensive earlier this year triggered the displacement of hundreds of thousands of civilians. The bloc called for an immediate halt to attacks on the city, an end to violence against civilians and ethnic communities, and unrestricted humanitarian access.

Meanwhile, a coalition of 29 countries expressed grave concern over the deteriorating situation, warning that approximately 500,000 civilians-including more than 100,000 internally displaced people-could face the risk of mass atrocities if fighting escalates.

The joint statement noted that at least 50 civilians had reportedly been killed during ten consecutive days of drone strikes in El Obeid and other parts of North Kordofan. It also highlighted reports of ethnically targeted violence, conflict-related sexual violence, and extensive damage to civilian infrastructure.

excerpt: Washington, D.C., June 28, 2026 - The United States has announced a new package of sanctions targeting individuals, entities, and sectors accused of prolonging Sudan's conflict, while introducing additional restrictions on Sudan's access to international financing and air transport.
title_en: US Imposes New Sanctions Targeting Sudan War Networks and State-Owned Airlines
excerpt_en: Washington, D.C., June 28, 2026 - The United States has announced a new package of sanctions targeting individuals, entities, and sectors accused of prolonging Sudan's conflict, while introducing additional restrictions on Sudan's access to international financing and air transport.
body_en:
Washington, D.C., June 28, 2026 - The United States has announced a new package of sanctions targeting individuals, entities, and sectors accused of prolonging Sudan's conflict, while introducing additional restrictions on Sudan's access to international financing and air transport.

The measures, announced by the U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC), target eight individuals and organizations accused of supporting the war through weapons procurement, explosives supply, and the recruitment of foreign fighters for both the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF).

U.S. officials said the sanctioned networks have contributed to extending the conflict, worsening the humanitarian crisis, and creating conditions that allow extremist groups to operate.

Washington also announced a second round of sanctions under the Chemical and Biological Weapons Control and Warfare Elimination Act. The measures include opposition to loans, financial assistance, and technical support for Sudan through international financial institutions, additional export restrictions, and a prohibition on Sudanese state-owned airlines operating flights to the United States.

The U.S. administration reiterated its call for an immediate humanitarian truce, urging both warring parties to cease hostilities, facilitate humanitarian access, and end attacks on civilians. It also called on foreign governments to halt all military and logistical support to the conflicting parties.

The latest measures follow recent legislative action in the U.S. Senate, where lawmakers approved legislation directing American representatives at international financial institutions to oppose loans and debt relief for Sudan, except for emergency humanitarian assistance. The proposed legislation also seeks to prohibit non-humanitarian foreign aid and restrict support for Sudanese government institutions and security forces.

The new sanctions build on earlier U.S. actions taken during the conflict. In 2025, Washington accused Sudan's government of violating the Chemical Weapons Convention through the alleged use of chemical weapons during the war. Earlier that year, the United States also designated the RSF and its commander, Mohamed Hamdan "Hemedti" Dagalo, under genocide-related sanctions.

Since the outbreak of the conflict, the United States has imposed multiple rounds of visa restrictions and economic sanctions targeting military leaders, former regime officials, and companies accused of financing or facilitating the war.

excerpt: Port Sudan, June 29, 2026 - Sudan and China have signed an agreement cancelling approximately $50 million in Sudanese debt, marking a new step in bilateral economic cooperation as Sudan continues to face mounting financial pressures.
title_en: China Cancels $50 Million of Sudan's Debt Amid Expanding Economic Cooperation
excerpt_en: Port Sudan, June 29, 2026 - Sudan and China have signed an agreement cancelling approximately $50 million in Sudanese debt, marking a new step in bilateral economic cooperation as Sudan continues to face mounting financial pressures.
body_en:
Port Sudan, June 29, 2026 - Sudan and China have signed an agreement cancelling approximately $50 million in Sudanese debt, marking a new step in bilateral economic cooperation as Sudan continues to face mounting financial pressures.

The agreement, signed in Port Sudan by Finance Minister Jibril Ibrahim and China's Chargé d'Affaires Xu Jian, provides for the cancellation of four interest-free loans owed by Sudan, totaling 344.52 million Chinese yuan (approximately $50 million).

The debt relief takes effect immediately, with the Central Bank of Sudan and the China Development Bank tasked with completing the financial settlement procedures associated with the cancelled loans.

Sudanese officials described the agreement as part of the longstanding economic partnership between the two countries and welcomed China's recent decision to eliminate customs duties on imports from 50 African nations, viewing the measure as an opportunity to strengthen trade relations.

The two sides also discussed expanding technical cooperation, including Chinese support for training Sudanese civil servants and strengthening institutional capacity across multiple sectors.

Chinese officials reaffirmed Beijing's commitment to supporting Sudan's economic recovery, reducing its debt burden, and deepening bilateral cooperation.

Discussions also reviewed progress on several Chinese-funded development projects, including the West Omdurman Abattoir, as well as the implementation of a previously announced 200 million yuan Chinese grant intended to finance projects in the energy, water, and agriculture sectors.

Officials further explored ways to improve banking cooperation between the two countries and examined the possible resumption of operations by the China National Petroleum Corporation (CNPC) in Sudan.

Port Sudan, June 18, 2026 - A high-level European Union delegation has concluded its first official visit to Sudan since the outbreak of the conflict in April 2023, signaling renewed diplomatic engagement as international efforts to end the war and address the country's worsening humanitarian crisis continue.

The two-day mission brought together 14 heads of EU diplomatic missions, led by the EU's representative to Sudan, Wolfram Vetter. The delegation held talks in Port Sudan and Khartoum with senior Sudanese officials, including the Chairman of the Sovereignty Council, his deputy, the Prime Minister, and other government representatives.

Discussions focused on the humanitarian situation, expanding access to aid, prospects for a ceasefire, and broader efforts to advance a political settlement to the conflict.

Following the visit, the delegation reaffirmed its solidarity with the Sudanese people and called on all parties to de-escalate the conflict as a first step toward a comprehensive ceasefire. The delegation also urged the creation of safe humanitarian corridors and protected zones to facilitate the delivery of assistance to civilians affected by the war.

EU representatives condemned attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure, particularly in El Fasher and Al Jazirah State, and called for an end to sieges that have restricted humanitarian access. They also reiterated support for Sudan's unity, sovereignty, and territorial integrity while opposing attempts to establish parallel governing structures.

The delegation further condemned the continued flow of weapons, mercenaries, and foreign fighters into Sudan and stressed the need to hold perpetrators of serious violations accountable.

The EU reaffirmed its support for international mediation efforts led by the African Union, the United Nations, the Intergovernmental Authority on Development (IGAD), the League of Arab States, and other international partners, encouraging Sudanese authorities to engage constructively with these initiatives in pursuit of an inclusive political process.

The visit has attracted significant attention as it marks the first return of senior EU diplomats to Sudan since the war began. Observers view the mission as an indication that the bloc is seeking greater direct engagement with developments inside the country after previously managing much of its diplomatic activity from outside Sudan.

excerpt_en: Kampala, June 2, 2026 - Uganda’s export earnings have surged to a record $10.2 billion during the 2025/26 financial year, up from $6.5 billion recorded over the same period a year earlier, driven largely by strong performances in coffee and gold exports.
body_en:
Kampala, June 2, 2026 - Uganda’s export earnings have surged to a record $10.2 billion during the 2025/26 financial year, up from $6.5 billion recorded over the same period a year earlier, driven largely by strong performances in coffee and gold exports.

title: Bank of Uganda Caps Cash Withdrawals in Drive Toward Digital Payments
excerpt: Kampala, June 3, 2026 - The Bank of Uganda (BoU) has announced new limits on over-the-counter cash withdrawals, beginning January 1, 2027, as part of a broader strategy to accelerate digital payments, reduce dependence on cash, and modernise the country’s financial system.
title_en: Bank of Uganda Caps Cash Withdrawals in Drive Toward Digital Payments
excerpt_en: Kampala, June 3, 2026 - The Bank of Uganda (BoU) has announced new limits on over-the-counter cash withdrawals, beginning January 1, 2027, as part of a broader strategy to accelerate digital payments, reduce dependence on cash, and modernise the country’s financial system.
body_en:
Kampala, June 3, 2026 - The Bank of Uganda (BoU) has announced new limits on over-the-counter cash withdrawals, beginning January 1, 2027, as part of a broader strategy to accelerate digital payments, reduce dependence on cash, and modernise the country’s financial system.

Under the new regulations, individual account holders will be limited to cash withdrawals of up to Shs50 million per day and Shs500 million per week. Corporate entities and businesses will face higher thresholds, capped at Shs250 million per day and Shs2.5 billion per week.

The central bank said the policy marks a significant shift in Uganda’s payments landscape, aimed at increasing transparency in financial transactions and encouraging wider adoption of digital financial services.

According to BoU, the withdrawal restrictions will apply to all accounts held with supervised financial institutions. However, transactions conducted through electronic payment channels, including Real Time Gross Settlement (RTGS) transfers and Electronic Funds Transfers (EFTs), will not be affected.

Authorities say the decision was informed by changing consumer behaviour and the rapid growth of electronic transactions across the country, with digital payment systems increasingly preferred for their efficiency and convenience.

The central bank noted that electronic credit transfers have become one of Uganda’s most widely used payment methods, reflecting growing public confidence in digital financial services among individuals, businesses, and government institutions.

BoU acknowledged that certain sectors of the economy continue to rely heavily on cash transactions and said safeguards would be introduced to avoid disrupting legitimate business activities.

Under the guidelines, supervised financial institutions will be required to establish risk-based customer profiles that may allow for differentiated withdrawal limits depending on a customer’s transaction history and business activities.

body_en:
Kampala, June 2, 2026 - Financial experts have called for reforms to Uganda’s digital payments tax system, proposing a reduction in the mobile money withdrawal tax from 0.5 percent to 0.25 percent amid growing signs that consumers are shifting to mobile and agency banking services to reduce transaction costs.

The proposal comes as mobile money continues to dominate Uganda’s digital payments ecosystem, with active accounts reaching 33.7 million by 2025 and annual transaction values nearing Shs195 trillion. The platform remains central to financial inclusion and everyday commerce, particularly for low-value, high-frequency transactions commonly used by households, small businesses, and informal sector operators.

Industry figures indicate that mobile money continues to play a critical role in Uganda’s economy, with millions of users relying on the service for daily financial transactions. However, experts argue that rising transaction costs, particularly withdrawal taxes, are increasingly influencing consumer behaviour.

Analysts say many users are gradually turning to agency banking and mobile banking platforms, which often offer lower transaction costs for similar services. Recent industry data shows agency banking transaction values increased significantly between 2024 and 2025, accompanied by substantial growth in transaction volumes and the number of registered agents across the country.

Experts argue that the trend reflects a broader structural shift in digital finance, with consumers increasingly opting for cheaper alternatives to avoid the cumulative impact of repeated withdrawal charges.

They further contend that Uganda’s current tax structure creates an uneven playing field because mobile money withdrawals attract higher taxation than comparable banking transactions, potentially distorting competition within the digital payments sector.

Tax specialists have also noted that Uganda imposes a comparatively heavier tax burden on mobile money withdrawals than several neighbouring East African countries, where excise duties are generally applied without additional withdrawal taxes.

While acknowledging the need for domestic revenue mobilisation, experts warn that excessive taxation could discourage the use of digital financial services and slow progress toward broader financial inclusion.

The delegation also reviewed ongoing national content and community development initiatives associated with the project. Thousands of Ugandans have participated in project activities, while investments in education, healthcare, agriculture, skills development, and access to clean water have been implemented in host communities.

Project developers reiterated their commitment to achieving first oil safely and efficiently while ensuring the development delivers lasting economic and social benefits for Uganda.

KAMPALA, June 26, 2026 - A proposed amendment to Uganda's Administration of Parliament Act has triggered intense political debate, with critics warning that the legislation could weaken the independence of the Leader of the Opposition (LoP) and alter the balance of power within Parliament.

The bill, introduced by Members of Parliament aligned with the Patriotic League of Uganda (PLU), seeks to revise the process for selecting and removing the Leader of the Opposition.

Among its reported provisions are proposals to allow independent Members of Parliament, alongside opposition legislators, to participate in electing the Leader of the Opposition and to establish procedures for the removal of a sitting LoP.

Supporters of the proposal argue that expanding participation in the election of the opposition leader would make the process more inclusive and democratic.

However, opponents contend that the changes could diminish the autonomy of the opposition, noting that many independent legislators are widely perceived to maintain close political ties with the ruling National Resistance Movement (NRM).

The proposal has revived debate over parliamentary reforms after a similar initiative introduced during the 11th Parliament failed to advance.

Political commentators argue that the current proposal comes at a time of shifting political alliances, raising broader questions about the future of parliamentary oversight and the role of the opposition in Uganda's multiparty political system.

Critics of the bill maintain that the proposed amendments could weaken Parliament's oversight function by reducing the institutional independence of the opposition, whose constitutional role includes holding the executive accountable.

excerpt: Bulange, Mengo, June 30, 2026 - Buganda Kingdom has launched a new disease surveillance committee in partnership with the Ministry of Health and the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) to improve monitoring and response to disease outbreaks and public health emergencies across the Kingdom.
title_en: Buganda Launches Joint Disease Surveillance Committee to Strengthen Outbreak Response
excerpt_en: Bulange, Mengo, June 30, 2026 - Buganda Kingdom has launched a new disease surveillance committee in partnership with the Ministry of Health and the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) to improve monitoring and response to disease outbreaks and public health emergencies across the Kingdom.
body_en:
Bulange, Mengo, June 30, 2026 - Buganda Kingdom has launched a new disease surveillance committee in partnership with the Ministry of Health and the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) to improve monitoring and response to disease outbreaks and public health emergencies across the Kingdom.

The committee, unveiled at Bulange following a briefing on Uganda’s Ebola situation, will be chaired by Buganda Minister for Information, Mobilisation and Kingdom Spokesperson Israel Kazibwe Kitooke. It brings together senior Kingdom officials tasked with strengthening early warning systems, coordination, and community-level reporting on health threats.

Speaking at the launch, Second Deputy Katikkiro Robert Waggwa Nsibirwa commended ongoing government efforts in managing outbreaks and urged local leaders to remain vigilant, including reporting activities such as bushmeat trade that may increase the risk of disease transmission. He emphasised the importance of community participation in safeguarding public health.

Ministry of Health officials reassured the public that Ebola remains under control, while cautioning against high-risk burial practices, particularly the washing of bodies of deceased persons, which can accelerate transmission. They said strengthened collaboration between government and cultural institutions will enhance surveillance and improve response capacity.

The new committee is expected to deepen coordination between health authorities and Kingdom structures, improve disease monitoring, and reinforce rapid response mechanisms for future public health emergencies.
